claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a chromium-enriched passive oxide layer.
The chromium-enriched passive oxide layer minimizes further chemical attack under aggressive conditions.
Typical steels used in these applications contain approximately 12–14% chromium.
These steels also contain nickel and molybdenum in established proportions.
These steels naturally form a passive film under ambient conditions.
Increasing chromium content or applying targeted surface treatments promotes a more uniform and adherent chromium oxide layer.
A chloride-containing acidic solution near 90°C and under moderate pressure mimics aggressive chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions.
Passive-film thickness, uniformity, and adhesion dictate resistance to corrosive attack.
Chromium in the alloy reacts with oxygen to form a thin, continuous, self-healing oxide layer.
The oxide layer blocks chloride ions and protons from reaching the underlying metal.
The oxide layer reduces ion transport and thereby limits the corrosion rate.
Increasing chromium content or improving film formation enhances the protective effect.
Enhanced chromium content or optimized surface treatment will produce a thicker, more uniform, and more adherent passive layer than the baseline.
The improved passive layer will significantly reduce corrosion rates relative to baseline samples.
Reduced chromium content or disrupted film formation will increase corrosion rates.
Existing baseline steels exhibit moderate corrosion resistance under typical operating conditions through passivation.
The proposed mechanism applies when passive-film formation governs corrosion resistance.
Mechanical loading or other environmental stresses may become dominant and limit the proposed mechanism's applicability.
